transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Hearing loss genetics, for Saturday, November 28.
Let's turn to Hearing loss genetics, where this week's papers are mostly about finding the right gene for the right family.
The largest one is from the Usami lab in Genes. A 158-gene panel in 18,475 Japanese patients found 29 patients from 22 families with candidate variants in P2RX2, the rare DFNA41 gene.
Most carried the same variant, c.1057G>A, a founder mutation. The loss started late, worsened over time, was often asymmetric, and may be linked to noise.
Because it's a founder allele, the yield will probably be lower outside Japan. And the noise link is only possible, not firm yet.

Next, from the Wang lab in the Journal of Translational Medicine. Exome sequencing of 83 Chinese families with dominant nonsyndromic hearing loss found POU4F3 variants in 9 of them, about 11 percent, all fully penetrant.

The surprise is that 60 percent of carriers had tinnitus, often before any measurable hearing loss. Truncating variants caused earlier, more severe loss. It's a small sample, but the authors argue POU4F3 should be prioritized on East Asian panels.

The third paper, from the Sun lab in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences, looks at recessive TMC1 patients with only one pathogenic variant after panel testing. Whole-genome sequencing found seven splice-altering variants and two recurrent deletions spanning exons 9 to 10.
That workflow, whole-genome sequencing then minigene and gap-PCR tests, could work for other recessive genes. A panel can easily miss deletions like those.
Three shorter ones. The Fu lab, in Genes, reports a homozygous LMX1A nonsense variant in a child from a consanguineous Yemeni family, though causality isn't proven.

The Dossena lab, in Biomolecules, proposes SCD5 as a candidate gene for enlarged vestibular aqueduct, based on a single patient. And the He lab, in Biomedicines, found only four small cohorts on mitochondrial variants and cisplatin ototoxicity, so that question is under-studied.
The takeaway is that deeper sequencing of large, ancestry-specific cohorts keeps finding causes that standard panels miss.
